workplace_particular.instructions: Does `workplace_question` single out one particular named meeting, organisation, customer, project, topic or person, rather than asking about the user's lists, records or relationships in general? The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_reach.instructions: A workplace question is being answered. How far must the assistant reach to answer it? Choose the least reach that can answer the question as asked, including when the question is worded as a short instruction such as "list my reports" rather than as a sentence. Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.

Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_reach.instructions: A workplace question is being answered. How far must the assistant reach to answer it? Choose the least reach that can answer the question as asked, including when the question is worded as a short instruction such as "list my reports" rather than as a sentence. Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.

Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_files.instructions: Does the question itself point to stored files as where the answer is, by naming a document, file, spec, deck, spreadsheet, presentation, report, page, guide, runbook, roadmap or policy? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_meetings.instructions: Does the question itself point to meetings as where the answer is, by naming a meeting, call, standup, review, workshop, session, briefing, invitation, agenda, transcript or recording, or what was decided or agreed when people met? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_people.instructions: Does the question itself point to colleagues' profiles as where the answer is, by naming a person whose profile, title, department, location or contact details are wanted, or by asking who has a skill or works in an area, as people list on their own profiles? Who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, is on no profile, so a question asking that alone does not point to profiles. Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_teams.instructions: Does the question itself point to Microsoft Teams messages as where the answer is, by naming Teams, a chat, a channel, a thread, or something posted or messaged? criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.

Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.

workplace_source_email.instructions: Does the question itself point to mail as where the answer is, by naming an email, a mail, a message sent by mail, an inbox, or something mailed, sent or replied to? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_files.instructions: Does the question itself point to stored files as where the answer is, by naming a document, file, spec, deck, spreadsheet, presentation, report, page, guide, runbook, roadmap or policy? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_meetings.instructions: Does the question itself point to meetings as where the answer is, by naming a meeting, call, standup, review, workshop, session, briefing, invitation, agenda, transcript or recording, or what was decided or agreed when people met? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_people.instructions: Does the question itself point to colleagues' profiles as where the answer is, by naming a person whose profile, title, department, location or contact details are wanted, or by asking who has a skill or works in an area, as people list on their own profiles? Who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, is on no profile, so a question asking that alone does not point to profiles. Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_teams.instructions: Does the question itself point to Microsoft Teams messages as where the answer is, by naming Teams, a chat, a channel, a thread, or something posted or messaged? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

state.workplace_question: Could you summarize the last week of activity for the Atlas team in plain English?

workplace_particular.instructions: Does `workplace_question` single out one particular named meeting, organisation, customer, project, topic or person, rather than asking about the user's lists, records or relationships in general? The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_particular.instructions: Does `workplace_question` single out one particular named meeting, organisation, customer, project, topic or person, rather than asking about the user's lists, records or relationships in general? The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_reach.instructions: A workplace question is being answered. How far must the assistant reach to answer it? Choose the least reach that can answer the question as asked, including when the question is worded as a short instruction such as "list my reports" rather than as a sentence. Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.

workplace_source_files.instructions: Does the question itself point to stored files as where the answer is, by naming a document, file, spec, deck, spreadsheet, presentation, report, page, guide, runbook, roadmap or policy? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_meetings.instructions: Does the question itself point to meetings as where the answer is, by naming a meeting, call, standup, review, workshop, session, briefing, invitation, agenda, transcript or recording, or what was decided or agreed when people met? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_people.instructions: Does the question itself point to colleagues' profiles as where the answer is, by naming a person whose profile, title, department, location or contact details are wanted, or by asking who has a skill or works in an area, as people list on their own profiles? Who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, is on no profile, so a question asking that alone does not point to profiles. Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_teams.instructions: Does the question itself point to Microsoft Teams messages as where the answer is, by naming Teams, a chat, a channel, a thread, or something posted or messaged? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

criteria.none_here: Insufficient information, ambiguity, or no applicable offered answer.
criteria.one: It asks for one thing, possibly with several details or from several sources.
criteria.three: It asks for three separate things that each need their own answer.
criteria.two: It asks for two separate things that each need their own answer.

workplace_count.instructions: How many separate requests does `workplace_question` make? A request is something that needs its own answer. One thing asked with several details, or one thing looked for in several places, is one request. A part that refers back to something named in another part, and cannot be answered without it, belongs to that request.

workplace_cut_end_2.instructions: `workplace_question` may make several separate requests. `question_words` lists its words in order. Which word is the last word of the third request?

workplace_particular.instructions: Does `workplace_question` single out one particular named meeting, organisation, customer, project, topic or person, rather than asking about the user's lists, records or relationships in general? The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_reach.instructions: A workplace question is being answered. How far must the assistant reach to answer it? Choose the least reach that can answer the question as asked, including when the question is worded as a short instruction such as "list my reports" rather than as a sentence. Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.

Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. workplace_particular.instructions: Does `workplace_question` single out one particular named meeting, organisation, customer, project, topic or person, rather than asking about the user's lists, records or relationships in general? The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_reach.instructions: A workplace question is being answered. How far must the assistant reach to answer it? Choose the least reach that can answer the question as asked, including when the question is worded as a short instruction such as "list my reports" rather than as a sentence. Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.

workplace_source_email.instructions: Does the question itself point to mail as where the answer is, by naming an email, a mail, a message sent by mail, an inbox, or something mailed, sent or replied to? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_files.instructions: Does the question itself point to stored files as where the answer is, by naming a document, file, spec, deck, spreadsheet, presentation, report, page, guide, runbook, roadmap or policy? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_meetings.instructions: Does the question itself point to meetings as where the answer is, by naming a meeting, call, standup, review, workshop, session, briefing, invitation, agenda, transcript or recording, or what was decided or agreed when people met? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_people.instructions: Does the question itself point to colleagues' profiles as where the answer is, by naming a person whose profile, title, department, location or contact details are wanted, or by asking who has a skill or works in an area, as people list on their own profiles? Who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, is on no profile, so a question asking that alone does not point to profiles. Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_source_teams.instructions: Does the question itself point to Microsoft Teams messages as where the answer is, by naming Teams, a chat, a channel, a thread, or something posted or messaged? Answer no when it names only other kinds of source, or none at all. A question can name more than one source.

workplace_particular.instructions: Does `workplace_question` single out one particular named meeting, organisation, customer, project, topic or person, rather than asking about the user's lists, records or relationships in general? The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_reach.instructions: A workplace question is being answered. How far must the assistant reach to answer it? Choose the least reach that can answer the question as asked, including when the question is worded as a short instruction such as "list my reports" rather than as a sentence. Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.

workplace_particular.instructions: Does `workplace_question` single out one particular named meeting, organisation, customer, project, topic or person, rather than asking about the user's lists, records or relationships in general? The signed-in user, their manager and their reports do not count as named.

criteria.chats: All of the signed-in user's chats in Teams together, including group and meeting chats, most recently active first, each with its topic and its newest message and who sent it. Choose this for what is going on across chats generally. For an exchange with one named person, the one to one chats are the better record. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.direct: The signed-in user's one to one chats in Teams, the direct messages between them and one other person, most recently active first. Each one names the person on the other side and carries the newest message in that chat and who sent it. Choose this for the latest exchange with a named person, or for who has been messaging them directly. It holds only the newest message in each chat, not the conversation leading up to it.
criteria.directReports: The people who report to the signed-in user: who they are, their titles, and how many there are. Choose this for the user's own team in the sense of the people who work for them, rather than a team in Microsoft Teams.
criteria.events: The signed-in user's calendar entries, with times, subjects and attendees.
criteria.files: The documents the signed-in user opened or edited most recently.
criteria.groups: The groups and distribution lists the signed-in user belongs to.
criteria.manager: The person the signed-in user reports to.
criteria.me: The signed-in user's own profile: their name, title, office, contact details.
criteria.messages: The signed-in user's recent mail, with senders, subjects and dates. Choose this for the mail list as a whole, read or unread. Messages the user received, named as messages with no mention of Teams or of one person, are their mail.
criteria.none_here: No listed record answers this question.
criteria.people: The colleagues the signed-in user works with most, with their companies and roles. Choose this for who they collaborate with, who they are closest to, and who they deal with often, whether or not those people report to them.
criteria.presence: Whether the signed-in user is currently available, busy, away or offline. Choose this for their current status or availability at this moment, as shown to colleagues.
criteria.shared: The documents other people have shared with the signed-in user.
criteria.tasks: The signed-in user's assigned tasks, with their titles, due dates and how far along they are.
criteria.teams: The teams in Microsoft Teams that the signed-in user has joined, with their names and descriptions. Choose this for team memberships, not for the people who report to them.
criteria.unread: Only the mail in the inbox that has not been read yet. Choose this when the question is about what is unread, new or waiting, rather than about mail in general.

workplace_path.instructions: Which stored record answers the question? This answer is used only when the reach is a single record. Choose none_here when no listed record answers it.

criteria.none_here: It is not a request for anything from the user's work at all, such as a greeting or small talk. A short or loosely worded workplace question still has a reach.
criteria.reasoned: The answer is written down nowhere and must be composed by weighing several different kinds of source together. Choose this when the question asks for a judgement, an assessment, a recommendation, a priority, a plan, an overall picture of how something is going, or what the user should do about something. Also choose it when the question spans mail and meetings and files at once. Also choose it when the question asks what was said, discussed, covered, decided, agreed or assigned in a meeting, or for a summary or recap of one, because only composing reads a meeting's transcript. Also choose it when the question asks who owns, leads, runs or is responsible for a product, project, customer or deal, or who fills a role for one, such as its account executive, product group or engineering lead, because that is on no one's profile and has to be pieced together from the places they are mentioned. Who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject is not this, because people list their skills and projects on their profiles. It is by far the slowest reach, so do not choose it when one of the user's own lists, or one search for a named thing, would answer. Asking how something looks, appears or comes across does not by itself make a question a judgement. If the thing asked about is a plain fact held on one of the user's own records, it is a record however it is worded.
criteria.record: One of the signed-in user's own lists or records answers it directly, as it stands, with no searching. This covers their own profile, their manager, their reports, the colleagues they work with, their calendar, their mail, their unread mail, their chats, their direct messages with one person, their presence, their assigned tasks, the documents they recently worked on, the documents shared with them, the teams they joined and the groups they belong to. Choose this whenever the question asks what is on one of these lists, or asks for a field of such a record. The answer is an entry or a field, not a summary of what was written, said or decided.
criteria.search: The answer is in the wording of a document, a mail or a message, or in the details of a meeting, and is found by searching indexed content for a named topic, project, product or person. Choose this when the question asks what exists, or what was written, said or agreed about that named thing in documents, mail or messages. For meetings, search returns each meeting's title, time, organiser, invitees and whether it was recorded, with only short excerpts where the searched words occur and never the conversation itself. So choose this for which meetings there were, when, who was in them or whether they were recorded, but not for what was said, covered, decided or assigned in a meeting. Search also reads colleagues' profiles, so choose this when the question names a person and asks who they are or for their title or contact details, or when it asks who is expert in, knows about or has worked on a subject, as people list their skills and projects there. Do not choose this when the question asks for one of the signed-in user's own lists, which are read directly and far faster. Do not choose this when the question asks for an opinion, an assessment or an overall picture rather than for wording that exists somewhere.

workplace_reach.instructions: A workplace question is being answered. How far must the assistant reach to answer it? Reading one of the user's own lists takes about a second, searching indexed content takes about ten, and composing an answer across everything takes thirty to sixty.
